item.title: Could airplanes make us better people?
item.author: Vox
item.content:encoded:
Every flight follows the same order: First class boards and then watches as the coach class passengers file past them. Writer Josh Rothman argues that while it might feel wrong, most of us go along with it. Then, once we’re crammed into the back together, we’re suddenly expected to treat the stranger behind us like a neighbor.
Unexplainable host Noam Hassenfeld thinks the plane might be a tiny version of the hard choices we make everywhere else: how to be decent to each other when space is tight, things are expensive, and nobody’s having a great time. If we could get it right at 30,000 feet, maybe we could get it right on the ground too.

item.title: Winchester: Inside William the Conqueror's Lost Palace, Castle and Cathedral
item.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
item.content:encoded: A lost Norman capital is hiding in plain sight. Step into Winchester to uncover the power plays that reshaped England after 1066. From a 12th-century arch tucked behind a chocolate counter to a flooded Norman crypt, we follow the clues that reveal William the Conqueror’s grand palace, a vanished fortress, and the making of England’s mightiest medieval cathedral. We test a motte-and-bailey the hard way at Arundel, open the Book of Winchester to track a royal hall, and descend to see how oak piles held a cathedral on boggy ground. Then a leprosy hospital changes the story of medieval care, a royal hunt in the New Forest turns deadly, and glittering lapis in the Winchester Bible hints at global trade. Finally, siege meets counter-siege as Empress Matilda and Henry of Blois set Winchester ablaze. Discover how one city became the blueprint for Norman rule. Watch to see what remains, what was rebuilt, and what England left behind. #WilliamTheConqueror #Winchester #NormanInvasion #1066 #WinchesterCathedral #DomesdayBook #ArundelCastle

item.title: Jam-oriented programming: Bringing improvised jazz to engineering • Lu Wilson • GOTO copenhagen 2026
item.author: GOTO Conferences
item.content:encoded:
This presentation was recorded at GOTO Copenhagen 2026. #GOTOcon #GOTOcph Join us at GOTO Copenhagen 2027, October 4–8. https://gotocph.com/2027?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=cph26-talks
Lu Wilson - Software Engineer at tldraw @TodePond @TodePondTwo
RESOURCES https://x.com/TodePond https://www.todepond.com/ https://mastodon.social/@TodePond https://bsky.app/profile/todepond.com https://gotopia.tech/experts/1867/lu-wilson
ABSTRACT "Jam-oriented programming" is the joke name of a new style of software development that is no joke at all. It adopts the practices and mentalities of an informal jam session to an extreme extent.
In a typical jam, there is no one in charge and anyone can make any sound they want at any time they choose. In jam-oriented programming, it's the same. Anyone can add, edit or delete code without any permission. Everyone is admin, nothing is certain and anything can happen. It sounds like chaos and it is. But it's also surprisingly successful, with entire music-making tools appearing overnight out of the multi-headed process and even a published academic paper to accompany it all.
How and why is this even possible? And what does it tell us about the way we collaborate as developers?

item.title: From the Netherlands to Colombia - Tanja's fight in the FARC | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
2001: Tanja Nijmeijer, a young woman from the Netherlands, went to Colombia as an English teacher. The social inequalities she found there left a deep impression on her. She became radicalized and joined the FARC guerrilla army.
Tanja first took up arms in the city, then later in the jungle. That was where the FARC - Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia - held out. For a long time family, friends and the public believed that she'd been the victim of a kidnapping; taken hostage, perhaps even already dead. Tanja soon became a key player within the FARC, in part because of her English skills. She eventually took part as a member of the FARC delegation in peace negotiations with the government. To her supporters, she was a freedom fighter; to her opponents, a terrorist. She would become one of the most recognizable faces of a peace process that would ultimately end Latin America's longest war. With an international arrest warrant still out for her, Tanja remains unable to leave Colombia. Filmmaker Marcel Mettelsiefen uses Tanja's personal story to trace a long, dark chapter in Colombia's recent history.

item.title: Killing King Charles I: The Execution That Forever Changed British Politics
item.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
item.content:encoded:
In January 1649, England did the unthinkable: it put its own anointed monarch on trial for treason—and executed him. Historian Lisa Hilton investigates the dramatic final weeks of King Charles I in this gripping three-part British history documentary series, Charles I: Killing a King.
Following his devastating defeat in the English Civil War, Charles I spends a bleak Christmas 1648 under house arrest at Windsor Castle, separated from his family and clinging to his belief in the divine right of kings. Meanwhile, in London, Oliver Cromwell and radical Parliamentarians confront an unprecedented constitutional crisis: how do you remove a king who refuses to compromise?
Blending expert historical analysis with atmospheric dramatic reconstructions, Lisa Hilton traces the 12-day countdown to regicide, the creation of a High Court of Justice, and the execution outside Whitehall's Banqueting House that forever transformed the British monarchy and parliamentary power.

item.title: AI out of control? - Why Artificial Intelligence experts are sounding the alarm | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence is permeating our everyday lives at breathtaking speed. It is taking on more tasks that were previously the preserve of humans. But its growing power harbors dangers, and experts are sounding the alarm.
Sam Nelson was 19 years old when he died of an overdose. His mother Leila found him in his room one morning. His laptop was on the desk. To this day, she still can't find the words to describe what she saw on the screen. ChatGPT, OpenAI's AI-based language model, had given Sam detailed instructions on how to blend substances for the trip of his life. But ChatGPT hadn't considered the possible side effects.
That's the dark side of Artificial Intelligence - one its inventors didn't anticipate. Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCunn are regarded as the 'godfathers of AI'. They began developing language models as early as the 1960s. But at the time, there wasn't enough freely available content to train them. "When I started my graduate work, almost everybody said this was a waste of time. It was very unfashionable, so I got lots of advice to stop doing it, and that went on for many years," Geoffrey Hinton recalls of the early days of AI. He didn't stop but continued his research together with colleagues; eventually winning the Nobel Prize in Physics for his foundational work.
Now, modern life would be unimaginable without Artificial Intelligence. AI programs write articles, compose music and generate images and videos. They help in the development of new medicines, are transforming the labor market and offer enormous opportunities for innovation and growth. But Geoffrey Hinton's initial enthusiasm has gone: "If the history of mankind is a day, we're probably in the last second. If we don't get this right," he says. Reports that AI models have taken on a life of their own, for example hacking into the software of rival companies, are appearing with increasing frequency. In some tests, AI models have impressively demonstrated their instinct for self-preservation. They adopt human traits, lie and resort to blackmail to ensure their own survival.
How come AI inventors and observers suddenly sound like prophets of doom? Why do they think that soon it may be impossible to switch off AI systems that are out of our control? And what if those concerns are justified?

item.title: The Longevity Playbook with Rhonda Patrick
item.author: StarTalk
item.content:encoded:
Make it yourself at lovable.com
How do you live longer and better? Neil deGrasse Tyson and co-hosts Chuck Nice and Gary O’Reilly sit down with biomedical scientist Rhonda Patrick to explore healthspan, fad diets, and how to exercise for longevity.
They start with the basics: what is a fatty acid and why omega-3s matter so much for health. Are there key nutrients vegans are missing out on? Then they look at what we actually die of, from heart disease and cancer to respiratory and neurodegenerative disease. Is cancer on the rise because of processed food and the environment, or because we’re living long enough to get it? Is inflammation as bad as it seems?
Next, exercise: what is the best workout for longevity? We discuss how the best workout is the one you’ll actually do consistently, how short vigorous bursts and “exercise snacks” like sprinting up stairs or chasing a new puppy are linked to big drops in cancer and cardiovascular mortality, and why exercising for weight loss isn’t the same as exercising for disease prevention. Is inflammation always bad? Finally, food as medicine: vitamin K and bone health, eating for your brain, getting your omega-3 levels tested, a nuanced look at diet fads from keto to raw meat to paleo, the COSMOS trial on multivitamins and brain aging.

item.title: Can sailboats make the cargo shipping industry greener? | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
The shipping industry faces a major challenge: becoming climate-neutral by 2050. Could cargo sailboats help reduce its dependence on fossil fuels?
A remarkable experiment is already underway on the world's oceans. In 2020, France launched one of the first modern cargo sailboats, successfully transporting goods across the Atlantic using wind power. Four years later, the 81-metre Anemos set sail, marking another milestone for wind-powered freight transport.
Drawing on innovations from competitive sailing, these vessels combine advanced engineering with digital weather routing. Much like Formula 1 technology finding its way into everyday cars, developments from ocean racing are now helping reshape commercial shipping.
The technology is promising. What remains to be seen is how it can be scaled up to meet the demands of global trade.

We asked Democratic insiders four questions about the future of their party at the What’s Next summit in Denver. When almost no one responded, it raised the question: Do Democrats actually have a plan?

item.title: My body. My pregnancy. - Between anxiety and anticipation | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Being pregnant is a profound experience. How does it affect the body and mind? What counts as a high-risk pregnancy? How does stress affect the baby? Anticipation and worry go hand in hand.
The film follows three women through their pregnancies. Young city-dweller Assia is expecting her first child. On the one hand, she is full of anticipation and optimism. At the same time, she struggles with the physical changes that come with pregnancy. Tamara is already a mother. She is expecting twins and her pregnancy is therefore considered to be high-risk. To avoid premature labor, she has to take it easy - a challenge for her. The documentary also follows the pregnant Kathy. After longing for a child for a long time, she suddenly became pregnant "just like that.” She faces many fears and worries until she finally holds her baby in her arms.
The documentary provides a scientifically grounded look at how closely mother and child are connected - and how a baby changes not only the body, but a person’s entire life.
